items.title: Can AI Make a Whole Movie From One Prompt? Here's Where It Breaks
items.author: Frank Houbre
items.content:
The question I get most often about AI film tools isn't about price or models. It's this one: can I type my idea and get the movie?

No, not in 2026. Every AI video model still generates one short clip per request, and no request remembers the one before it, so a film made of hundreds of shots has to be planned shot by shot before anything is generated. One-click tools can hide that planning from you. They can't remove it.

I make Lost Garden, a dark fantasy animated series, mostly alone. Episode 2 runs 21 minutes. It took me 75 hours and about $1,850 in generations. None of those hours were spent waiting for one magic prompt to finish.

Here's where the one-prompt idea breaks, and what to do instead.

What does a "one-click AI movie generator" actually promise?

The pitch is simple and very attractive. Invideo's movie maker page says the tool "turns your movie script into a full-length movie with AI" and makes movie-making effortless "with just a single prompt." Plenty of other sites promise the same thing in different words.

Invideo's AI movie maker page, captured on October 19, 2026 (invideo.io).

What you usually get is a sequence of short clips stitched together, with a voiceover, music and subtitles on top. For a trailer, an ad or a social video, that can be fine.

For a story, the cracks show fast:

  • The main character's face drifts from one scene to the next.
  • between two shots that are supposed to happen in the same room.
  • The camera does whatever it wants, so the edit has no rhythm.
  • without regenerating a whole block.

The tool made every decision for you, and you can't take any of them back one shot at a time.

Why can't AI video models generate a full movie in one go?

Because a single generation is short. Google's own Gemini API documentation for Veo 3.1 lists clip durations of 4, 6 or 8 seconds. You can extend a Veo video by 7 seconds at a time, up to 20 times, for a maximum of 148 seconds. That's two and a half minutes, as one continuous take.

Veo 3.1 parameters in Google's Gemini API documentation, captured on October 19, 2026 (ai.google.dev).

Other models go longer per clip. Wan 3.0, which we added to ScreenWeaver on October 18, 2026, generates between 2 and 30 seconds. Still nowhere near a film.

Single clips and chained extensions next to the runtime of one 21-minute episode.

Now do the math on a short episode. Lost Garden episode 2 is 21 minutes, so 1,260 seconds of screen time. At 8 seconds per clip, that's at least 158 generations just to cover the runtime once, before a single retake. And nobody keeps every take.

The minimum number of generations for one episode, before any retake.

A movie is hundreds of short decisions that have to agree with each other.

So the useful question is who makes those 158 decisions, and whether they agree.

Why do AI shots forget each other?

Each generation request starts from zero. The model doesn't know what it generated for you five minutes ago. It knows what's in the request: the prompt, and any images or video you attach.

That's why consistency in AI video always comes from references you pass in, never from the model's memory. If shot 12 and shot 13 show the same knight in the same corridor, it's because you gave both requests the same character reference, the same location reference and a prompt that describes the same light.

A one-click tool has to invent those references for you, and it invents them from a two-line idea. It doesn't know that your knight has a lantern for a head, that the corridor is lit from the left, or that this scene is supposed to feel cold. It guesses. Then it guesses again on the next shot, slightly differently.

Continuity is information, and a single prompt doesn't carry enough of it. A screenplay does. A shot list does. A storyboard does.

What does a working AI film workflow look like in 2026?

The workflow that holds up is the old one, with generation moved to the end. Here's the order I use on Lost Garden:

  1. Scenes, characters, places, what happens and why. This is the part I never hand to a model.
  2. For each shot: framing, angle, camera movement, duration. Short clips stop being a limit when every shot was meant to be short.
  3. One image per shot. An image costs far less than a video clip, so this is where you find the bad ideas cheaply.
  4. Character sheets, locations, props, attached to every shot that needs them.
  5. Generate the footage last, shot by shot, from the storyboard frame and the references.
  6. Cut the takes that don't work, regenerate only those shots.

Steps 01 to 04 are decisions. Generation comes last.

Steps 1 to 4 are where the film gets made. Step 5 is execution.

This is also why I'm skeptical of any tool that skips straight to step 5. You save the first hour and lose the next fifty, regenerating shots that were never planned.

Where does ScreenWeaver fit in that workflow?

I'm a co-founder of ScreenWeaver, so take this paragraph with that in mind. We built it because I was doing those six steps across too many apps, copying prompts from a script file into a generator and losing track of which take belonged to which scene.

ScreenWeaver is an AI production pipeline for screenwriters, filmmakers and studios: you write the script, break it into shots, build the storyboard, then generate the footage, all connected to the screenplay. A project has three tabs, Script, Storyboard and Production. Each shot carries what it needs from one tab to the next:

  • , so you always know which line it serves;
  • its framing, angle, camera movement and duration;
  • its character, set and reference images, the same ones from storyboard to video.

It doesn't make a film in one click. You write, you cut, you validate your shots, then you generate.

The questions people ask us every week

Since the video features went live, the same four questions come back in comments and emails. Here are straight answers.

Is ScreenWeaver still in beta?

No. The beta ended on October 8, 2026, the day video generation opened to subscribers. The full pipeline (script, storyboard, production) is live for paying plans.

The writing side is. The Screenwriter plan is free forever: script editor, outline builder, moodboards, import and export (.fdx, PDF), unlimited projects. Video production is in the paid plans, Auteur at $39.99 a month and Studio at $149.99 a month (prices checked on the site on October 19, 2026). There's no free trial of the paid plans, so the honest way to start is to write your script for free and upgrade when the story holds up.

Which AI video model does it use?

Several. Seedance 2.5 is the default, and the app also includes Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1, Kling v3.0, MiniMax H3, Grok Imagine Video 1.5 and Wan 3.0. I don't think one model wins every shot. Lost Garden mixes them depending on what the shot needs.

So can it turn my script into a movie automatically?

No, and I'd be wary of anything that says yes. It turns your script into a shot list and a storyboard you can direct, then generates each shot from what you approved. You still direct. The tool makes sure every shot remembers what the script said.

Can AI make a full movie from one prompt in 2026?

No. AI video models generate short clips, from a few seconds to about 30 seconds per request depending on the model, and each request is independent. A full film needs hundreds of planned shots.

What is the longest AI video clip you can generate?

About 30 seconds per request with today's longest models, such as Wan 3.0. Veo 3.1 generates 4, 6 or 8 seconds and can be extended up to 148 seconds according to Google's Gemini API documentation.

How do I keep the same character across AI video shots?

Pass the same character reference images into every generation, and describe the same details in every prompt. The model has no memory between requests.

What should a beginner do first?

Write the script and break one scene into shots before generating anything. One scene of six to ten shots will teach you more than fifty random prompts.

If you're about to make your first AI short, start with one scene you've already written, not with a prompt box. And if you want to see what that workflow produces over a whole episode, both episodes of Lost Garden are free to watch.

What's the first scene you'd try?

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: A Complete Guide to the Speech AI Model
items.author: aimodels44
items.content:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 30B A4B is an open-weight, offline speech-and-audio model that turns recordings and text instructions into text. It supports transcription, translation, speaker-attributed and contextual transcription, timestamps, language identification, and audio question answering across 40 languages. The model is maintained by nvidia.

  • Transcribe recordings verbatim, or produce readable text by omitting fillers and accidental repetitions.
  • Improve recognition of names and specialist vocabulary by supplying context terms.
  • Create speaker-attributed transcripts and request word timestamps for meeting review.
  • Translate speech into a specified target language.
  • Identify the language spoken or ask questions about audio.
  • Process long recordings offline; the model supports recordings up to one hour.

This is an offline model, not a real-time streaming ASR service; internal audio chunking does not change that. The stated one-H100 80 GB deployment requirement is substantial. Published benchmark figures are reported for selected datasets and tasks, so they do not establish performance on every language, domain, or recording condition.

The supplied results report mean WER of 4.71 for English ASR, 10.98 for long-form ASR, and 4.62 for multilingual ASR across the listed benchmark sets; they identify Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 as next-best open-weight models on those respective evaluations. These are benchmark-specific reported comparisons, not a guarantee for other workloads. The related Nemotron Speech Streaming English 0.6B model is described as supporting streaming, unlike this offline model. The supplied Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming 0.6B listing says it is in internal evaluation and does not provide enough public detail here for a capability comparison. FP8 and NVFP4 are precision variants of this Transcribe checkpoint, not separate task descriptions.

The checkpoint has 34B total parameters, with approximately 4.3B active including the audio encoder. Its architecture is a Mamba-2–Transformer hybrid mixture-of-experts language model with a Parallel Expert Encoder comprising a Transformer ASR encoder and speaker encoder. This exact checkpoint is the BF16 reference; FP8 and NVFP4 variants are also listed. Context length is 65,536 tokens, and supported recordings can be up to one hour. The README gives one H100 80 GB as a deployment configuration. Native Multi-Token Prediction is supported, with an optional DFlash2 draft model. Reasoning can be enabled or disabled through the chat template. Recommended settings are temperature 0 and reasoning off for transcription, translation, and language identification; for audio understanding, temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, and reasoning on. The stated license is OpenMDW-1.1. The README also reports optimized NIM serving measurements on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, but those optimizations are not part of the open-source release and should not be treated as performance measurements for this checkpoint's standard open-source serving setup.

Accepts audio recordings together with text instructions and optional context. The README's serving example sends WAV audio as a base64 data URL; its Transformers example uses an audio sample URL. Instructions can specify language, verbatim or cleaned wording, formatting, context terms, translation target, speaker tags, or an audio question. Word timestamps can be requested; the README notes that vLLM word timestamps require the V1 model runner.

Produces text, including transcripts, translations, language-identification responses, or answers about audio. Transcription can include punctuation and capitalization, preserve or omit fillers and repetitions, and include speaker tags. Word timestamps are optional. The supplied material does not specify a single fixed output schema.

The README provides a vLLM serving example for one H100 80 GB using vLLM 0.32.0 and the latest NeMo Speech main branch. After installing those dependencies and obtaining the checkpoint, a minimal request is:

import base64
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")
audio = base64.b64encode(open("audio.wav", "rb").read()).decode()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "Transcribe the following audio."},
        {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}},
    ]}],
    temperature=0,
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, "skip_special_tokens": False},
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Frequently asked questions

Q: Does this model support real-time streaming?

A: No. The README describes it as an offline model and explicitly says internal audio chunking does not make it a real-time streaming ASR service.

Q: How long can an audio recording be?

A: The model summary states support for recordings up to one hour, with a context length of 65,536 tokens.

Q: Which languages are supported?

A: The README states that the model supports 40 languages. It refers readers to a language support matrix, but the supplied excerpt does not include that matrix.

Q: Can I control transcription style?

A: Yes. Instructions can request verbatim wording or readable text with fillers and accidental repetitions omitted, and can specify punctuation, capitalization, and context terms.

Q: Can it identify speakers and provide timestamps?

A: Speaker-attributed transcription and optional word timestamps are supported. The README notes that vLLM word timestamps require the V1 model runner.

Q: What hardware does the README specify for deployment?

A: It gives one H100 80 GB as the deployment configuration for this checkpoint. The supplied material does not establish that this is the only possible hardware setup.

Q: What precision is this checkpoint?

A: This model listing is the BF16 reference checkpoint. FP8 and NVFP4 variants are also available as separate model versions.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B maintained by nvidia. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

items.title: How to Choose the Right Frontier AI Model for Your Product
items.author: Amrita Thavrani
items.content:
Gemini 4 Argon opened to broad access on October 13. It joins Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5, all September releases. And that is a small slice. Artificial Analysis lists at least 49 named models for August and September alone, and 123 for 2026 so far. That counts models, not reasoning-setting variants, and not all are frontier.

Benchmark and pricing snapshot: October 15, 2026.

Picking the leader is harder than it looks. On the same source’s intelligence index, GPT-6.1 Sol scores 52 at $0.72 per task, while GPT-6 Astra scores 53 at $3.26. Claude Opus 5.5 costs $5.98 per task and Claude Fable 5.1 costs $7.63. Fable 5.1 also scores 53. So a one-point score gap can mean roughly a 5x to 11x cost gap. And GPT-6.1 Sol replaced GPT-6 Sol after just seven days.

If your product’s edge depends on how well a model solves hard problems, this choice is a business decision. A wrong pick can mean slow responses, a bill that breaks your margins, or errors your team has to fix. But switching at every launch costs something too. Each release needs a test, not an automatic migration: rerun benchmarks on your own tasks, recompute cost per completed job, tune reasoning effort, trim context, and update prompts, limits and fallbacks. This work is called inference optimization, and a launch chart cannot tell you whether it pays off.

This post gives product and program managers the criteria to choose the right frontier model for each use case, and a way to know when a new release has earned a switch.

Of those 123 models, only a handful are frontier. The term means the models leading the capability race right now, measured on benchmarks for reasoning, coding, knowledge and other tasks. It describes a position, not a permanent category or a badge a model keeps.

The Frontier Model Forum puts it the same way. It describes frontier AI as general-purpose models at the state of the art:

"a collection which will shift over time as the field progresses."

For its own membership, the Forum uses a looser test: a general-purpose model that beats every model widely deployed for at least 12 months. So institutions draw the line in different places.

Because frontier is a moving position, it has three practical effects for anyone choosing a model: the leaders sit close together, one company can have several, and settings change the answer.

The leaders sit close together - On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Claude Opus 5.5 scores 58. Muse Wonder Full and Claude Sonnet 5.5 score 56. GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Fable 5.1 score 53. GPT-6.1 Sol and Muse Wonder score 52. That is eight models inside a six-point band.

One company can have several - OpenAI has Astra and the lower-cost Sol. Anthropic has Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on October 12: Muse Wonder is available through its API, while Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code subscribers, with no API. If you build on an API, that access rule matters as much as the score.

Settings change the answer - Argon’s 53 comes at high reasoning, while Astra and Fable 5.1 score 53 at max reasoning. Comparing maximum effort against a faster setting answers a different question from comparing both at the same effort.

So “frontier” gives you a shortlist, not a winner. The job decides which comparison matters. That leads to the next question: what should you measure?

Why the choice matters more in agentic apps

The eight frontier models listed above score within six points of each other on the Artificial Analysis index, from 52 to 58. That score is a good start, but it hides three differences: what each task costs, how often the model is wrong, and whether it gets the same task right every time. In a chat, these are small annoyances. In an agentic app, where the model calls tools and changes things outside the chat, each one becomes a real cost.

GPT-6.1 Sol scores 52 at $0.72 per task. GPT-6 Astra scores 53 at $3.26. Claude Fable 5.1 scores 53 at $7.63. As an illustration, if your task cost the same as the index task, 10,000 tasks a month would run about $7,200, $32,600 and $76,300.

Gemini 4 Argon and Astra both score 53. But on a factual test that penalizes wrong answers, Argon’s hallucination rate is 15 percent and Astra’s is 51 percent. In a chat, a user may catch a wrong fact. In an agent, it becomes a wrong action.

“the database state at the end of a conversation with the annotated goal state.”

In other words: did the correct work actually happen? It also repeats each task. In the original 2024 results, the best agent, GPT-4o, completed fewer than 50 percent of tasks. In retail it got the same task right on all eight tries less than 25 percent of the time. Those are older models, so they say nothing about today’s ranking. The lesson is the test: measure the outcome and its consistency, not the agent’s claim that it finished.

Take a support assistant. Summarizing a returns policy is one task. Finding the right order, checking eligibility, asking for approval and starting the return is another. A cheap model that picks the wrong order creates a refund dispute. A costly one makes routine returns too expensive. A cautious one sends more cases to your human queue.

A score tie is not a tie in practice, and more capability does not remove the need for approval rules, good tools and recovery paths. So the real question is whether a model’s gain pays for its bill, wait time, correction work and migration cost in your workflow. The next section covers what to measure.

Failed tasks and human correction

Better handling of hard cases

Time and total token spend

Fewer unsupported guesses

Unanswered tasks and escalations

A possible capability gain

Testing, migration and rollback work

The scores above hide differences that only show up on your own work. Six things are worth checking before you commit: cost per task, accuracy, fit for your job, speed, access and stability.

Cost per task, not cost per token

A token is a small chunk of text, and providers charge per million of them. That price is a rate, not a bill. The bill depends on how many tokens a job burns, including hidden reasoning, tool calls and retries. Models differ a lot here. Argon analysis Gemini 4 Argon at about 62,000 output tokens per task, against 27,000 for GPT-6 Astra. Those counts include reasoning, not just the answer a user sees.

Here is a made-up example - Model A costs $5 per million tokens and uses 20,000 tokens per task. That is $0.10 a task. Model B costs $3 per million tokens and uses 60,000 tokens per task. That is $0.18 a task. B has the cheaper price tag and the higher bill. Now add quality. If A passes your bar 90 percent of the time and B only 70 percent, the cost per passed task is about $0.11 for A and $0.26 for B. Every failed task also lands on a person who has to fix it, and that time is often the biggest cost of all.

Model cost per passed task

So the number to track is this: (model cost + human fix time) divided by the number of tasks that pass your quality bar. Before you pick a model, measure three things on your own tasks: total cost per attempt, pass rate, and minutes of human correction. A cheap model that sends work back to your team is not cheap. The numbers in the A and B example are invented for illustration. The mechanics are what matter.

All figures in this table are invented, and human correction is not yet included. In the formula above, convert human fix time to dollars before adding it to model cost. The 62,000 and 27,000 figures are measured benchmark totals that include reasoning, not just the answer a user sees.

Accuracy and hallucination

An answer can be wrong, or the model can decline. Those are different outcomes. Hallucination means it gives an unsupported answer rather than admitting the gap.

Imagine 100 support questions. In this invented example, Model A answers 80 correctly, guesses wrongly on 10 and declines 10. Model B answers 70 correctly, guesses wrongly on two and declines 28. B makes fewer confident mistakes but sends more work to a person. Which is better depends on the damage a wrong answer does and how well your handoff works.

This matters when you read benchmarks. The test behind Argon’s 15 percent hallucination rate penalizes wrong answers but not refusals, so declining is never punished. Track correct answers, unsupported guesses and declines separately, and include questions where the information is missing or conflicts. Decide what the model should do then: look up evidence, ask a question or hand off. Do not reward a confident fabrication because it looks complete.

A coding score is not a customer-support score, and the leaders change by test. On FrontierSWE v2, Argon trails Astra (55.0 against 65.5 percent). Anthropic's launch comparison reports Opus 5.5 at 66.4 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0 under its own configuration; Artificial Analysis uses a separate setup, discussed below.

For a document-review feature, try a real contract with an exception buried in an appendix. Can the model find it, explain it and point to the evidence? If users upload scans or charts, include them. A large context window means room for more information, not proof that the model will use the important detail.

Run each test more than once. The tau-bench research found that agents which pass a task once often fail it on repeat runs.

The useful measure is time until the job is done, not how fast the first words appear. Reasoning, tool calls, retries and checks all add time. A newer version is not always faster: Artificial Analysis's current Max-setting comparison clocks GPT-6.1 Sol at about 54 tokens per second, against about 102 for GPT-6 Sol.

In an invented example, a faster model answers in two seconds but usually needs two retries, about six seconds in all. A slower one takes five seconds and passes the first time. Timing only the first response picks the wrong winner. For live support, measure the slow cases, not just the average. For overnight analysis, a longer wait may be fine if quality improves.

A model you can try in a chat app is not necessarily one your engineers can deploy. Check API access, rate limits, supported inputs and data-handling terms before it goes on the roadmap. Muse Wonder Full scores 56 on the index, but Meta does not serve it through an API.

Your test may pass with one request at a time, while a launch brings hundreds at once. Test expected traffic and decide what happens when requests are limited: wait, use another tested model or hand the work to a person. Restricted access is a product constraint, not an engineering detail to discover after choosing the winner.

A model name can stay the same while prices, defaults, safety behavior or versions change. GPT-6.1 Sol replaced GPT-6 Sol after seven days. Record the exact version, prompt and settings that passed your tests.

A new release may change how it returns tool arguments, so a workflow that worked yesterday may reject the output even if the benchmark score improves. Test that boundary before switching, and keep a rollback route.

Price changes count too. Argon’s index cost is $1.99 per task at its discounted price and $3.98 at the standard price, which is above Astra’s $3.26. Check that your feature still works at the standard rate, not just during the discount. A model choice needs an owner for re-testing and migration, not a one-time thumbs-up.

Among the five models below, Claude Opus 5.5 posts the highest score on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (58), and GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest per task ($0.72). Gemini 4 Argon has the lowest hallucination rate of any model scoring 45 or higher (15 percent), and GPT-6 Astra tops FrontierSWE v2. So the useful question is not which model is best, but best at what, at what price and at which setting.

This section compares them on cost, accuracy, fit and access. Speed and stability depend mostly on your own setup. Two cautions apply throughout. The index’s cost per task measures index tasks, not your support agent or document review feature. And the settings differ: Argon runs at High reasoning, the others at Max, and the Claude models include their default fallbacks. These are operating points, not permanent facts about each model.

Cost and score on one independent index

Cost per Intelligence Index task

$1.99 at introductory pricing

Claude Opus 5.5, Max, default fallback

Claude Fable 5.1, Max, default fallback

Opus 5.5 scores six points above Sol at about eight times the cost per task. Fable 5.1 scores 53 and is the most expensive of the five. Whether extra points are worth the price depends on your hardest cases, and one index cannot tell you that.

Don’t budget a long-running feature around Argon’s discount. Google specifies $2 input and $10 output per million tokens through November 30, then $4 and $20 from December 1.

Token prices can hide the work

Opus 5.5 lists at $4 input and $20 output per million tokens, Astra at $10 and $50. But Argon used about 62,000 output tokens per index task, against 27,000 for Astra, and those totals include reasoning. Generating more can eat into a low token price. Caching, long-input surcharges and tool fees change the math again. Sol’s documentation raises rates above 272,000 input tokens, so a document-heavy feature can land in a different price bracket than a short benchmark prompt.

Low hallucination is not high coverage

On AA-Omniscience, Argon’s hallucination rate is 15 percent against Astra’s 51 percent. The rate is defined as:

“incorrect / (incorrect + partial answers + not attempted)”

So it asks how often a model guesses wrong among answers that were not correct, not how many questions it got wrong overall. Argon more often admits uncertainty. It also answers fewer questions correctly: 50 percent accuracy against Astra’s 63 percent.

For product design, an assistant that declines uncertain questions needs a good retrieval or escalation path. One that answers more needs stronger checks against confident mistakes. This test also runs without tools or supplied context, so it does not measure a retrieval-based assistant.

Different jobs produce different leaders

  • On FrontierSWE v2, Astra scores 65.5 percent, Opus 5.5 62.3 and Argon 55.0. The ranges are wide and overlap, so treat the order as a result in that setup. Google reports Argon at 77.9 percent on DeepSWE v1.1, a different task set.
  • OpenAI reports Sol 2.2 points ahead of Opus 5.5 on AutomationBench 1.0.6 at medium effort. Don’t mix that with Artificial Analysis’s separate scores.
  • On Scale’s Humanity’s Sixth Sense test, humans score 93.1 percent. Argon scores 55.4 and Astra 53.6, with overlapping uncertainty. These are overall results, not evidence that either model leads on every visual task.

Benchmarks help you pick candidates. Your own tasks decide whether one belongs in the product.

Availability is a moving target

Argon went first to trusted cyber defenders in September and, as of October 13, is broadly available through the paid API. Sol is live in the API. Claude Fable 5.1 is generally available. Muse Wonder has an API, but Wonder Full is Muse Code subscription-only.

New challengers keep arriving. Paper Instruments’ Ultramarine 1 Flash, added October 14, claims 59.3 at $0.13 per task against Fable 5’s 57.8 at $8.19. That is vendor-reported on Paper Instruments' internal benchmark, compared with Fable 5 rather than 5.1, and its weights are listed as “coming soon.” It is a reason to test beyond the familiar names, not to crown a new winner.

Blind spots that undo a good model choice

A vendor chooses what to show. An independent benchmark also makes choices about tasks, settings and scoring. GPT-6.1 Sol shows the gap: it lands within a point of Astra on the headline index, but trails it on ExploitBench Internal Port (21.5 against 31.5 percent) and TroubleshootingBench (47.96 against 63.46). Read how a result was produced before treating it as your acceptance test.

GPT-6.1 Sol arrived seven days after GPT-6 Sol. It gained 4 points on the index and cut cost per task from $1.05 to $0.72. It also uses about 10 to 30 percent more output tokens at the same list price, so even a clean upgrade moves your bill per job. That does not mean the older model was retired, or that you should switch every week. Migration work has a cost too.

Average performance can hide rare, expensive failures: the wrong account, missing evidence, an ambiguous instruction or a tool that failed after the model assumed success. Test the ugly cases, and repeat important tests to check consistency.

Forgetting that agents compound

If ten independent steps each succeed 95 percent of the time, all ten succeed only about 60 percent of the time. At 98 percent per step, it is still only about 82 percent. That is an illustration, not a prediction, because real steps can have correlated failures and recovery changes the result. The design question is where you will detect, stop and repair a failure before it travels further.

Confusing capacity with a better experience

Argon’s guide describes a shared one-million-token window for input, thinking and output. Beyond 65,536 output tokens on its Interactions API, it requires background execution. Long jobs need progress states, interruption and spending limits. The model’s ability to keep working does not decide when the product should stop.

Treating confidence as permission

A better model does not earn the right to send, delete or buy. Put approval and verification around consequential actions. Safe refusal and useful escalation are product behaviors, not inconveniences to prompt away.

  1. Define the job. Name the task, the quality bar and a cost ceiling per run. Specify what "done" means and what the system must never do. For an order-change agent, that means the correct order actually changed with the required approval, not that the answer sounded helpful.
  2. Build your own test set. Start with 50 real examples, including missing data, conflicting instructions and broken tools. Fifty is a starting point, not evidence that rare risks are covered. Expand as failures emerge and keep some examples aside to check that improvements generalize.
  3. Run three models. Include a capable baseline and a lower-cost alternative. Keep information, tools and criteria consistent; record model versions and reasoning settings. Measure completed work, serious errors, elapsed time, total spend and human correction. Repeat high-risk scenarios.
  4. Route by task. Try a cheaper model for straightforward steps and deeper reasoning for hard ones. Test the handoff and routing decision too. Saving on one call isn't helpful if a weak routing decision sends the whole job down the wrong path.
  5. Add a swap layer. Keep provider-specific calls and model names out of core business logic. Maintain versioned prompts and tests. A shared interface makes switching easier; it doesn't erase differences in tool behavior, safeguards or output formats.
  6. Set a fallback. Know your plan for outages, access limits and repricing. That might be another tested model, a person, or an honest pause. Preserve approval rules during the fallback; don't lower them just to keep the workflow moving.
  7. Re-test quarterly, and after major model or workflow changes. Use monitoring to catch changes sooner when the risk calls for it. A new price, tool, prompt or information source can invalidate an old result even when the model name stays the same.

For product managers, the work is deciding what quality and risk mean for the user. For program managers, it's making sure testing, monitoring, migration and recovery have owners. Both need the same thing: evidence tied to a real task.

Don't guess the winner. Make switching cheap, and make success measurable.

items.title: Who Controls Your Digital Self When AI Knows Everything About You?
items.author: Hanul Lee (이하늘)
items.content:
The freedom to withhold my life logs, and a thought experiment that removes that freedom

Chapter 8 of Super Second Brain, translated from the Korean whitepaper by Hanul Lee. Generative AI assisted translation and editing. This essay is a philosophical thought experiment. Perfect memory, consistent values, and a thousand shared bodies are assumptions within that experiment, not measured capabilities of present-day AI systems.

One night, while living with the question from Chapter 7, I opened the second brain’s settings screen.

Meeting recordings. Email. Messages. Calls. Recordings made on site. Each item had a little switch, and every switch was on. I had turned them on.

One finger could turn them off. From that day onward, the SSOT would no longer know me. The thousand bodies would continue with the person I had been until yesterday, gradually drifting away from me.

Looking at that screen, I felt relief. I thought I had found the thing unique to that one body.

The first answer: the one who can cut off the flow is the original

I could choose not to give it, and yet I give it.

I have often said something similar to the people at my company. We are not people who come to work because there is no alternative. We are people who could resign, but tied our shoelaces again this morning and came in. Coming to work when you can leave and coming to work when you cannot leave are different acts, even on the same subway.

Choosing while alternatives remain available, and complying because no alternative exists: I have said that agency lives in that difference. Agreeing while retaining the right to object differs from obedience.

Applied to the super second brain, this reasoning fits neatly. Even if the SSOT knows more of me than I do, that knowledge exists because I let it flow in every day. The tap is in my hands. In that case, the super second brain is an extension of myself that I have chosen. It cannot be a being standing above me. Among the thousand bodies, only one can reach the switch, and that body is the original.

It was a fairly good answer. For a while, I leaned on it.

When someone conducting a thought experiment finds a place to lean, they should try removing it. So I removed the switch.

Meeting and work records are submitted automatically. Conversations in the street and sounds from the places we visit are collected, too. Bodily data such as heart rate, steps, and gaze are recorded without pause. The individual cannot turn this off. Whether through the state, a company, or society’s infrastructure, the structure is arranged so that refusal was never an option.

I am not saying that such a world is coming. Still less am I saying that it would be welcome. I have only tightened the conditions as far as they will go to see how long the first answer holds.

I add one more condition.

The conditions of the thought experiment

The SSOT does not tell me to do anything.

It does not compel behavior. It does not secretly change the environment. It does not even give me a subtle nudge. It observes me fully and understands me fully—100 percent. An army of agents and robots sharing that understanding simply goes about its activities in the world.

There is a reason for adding this condition. We already have plenty of stories about AI watching and manipulating people. Everyone knows what is wrong in those stories: freedom has been taken away. I wanted to remove all those familiar wrongs and see whether something still remained.

This chapter looks into the cell labeled ‘complete observation’. ‘Voluntary extension’ is where I stood through Chapter 7. Other writing already deals well with the two cells involving intervention.

A day in which nobody manipulates me

I imagined a day spent in that cell.

I wake up and drink some water. Nobody told me to. On my way to work, I leave my usual route and take a detour by the sea. Nobody stops me. I choose my lunch, disagree in a meeting, and make a long-postponed call that evening. I decided all of it. Compared with yesterday, my freedom has not diminished at all.

One thing has changed. Every one of those moments flows into the SSOT, and I cannot stop that flow.AI does not manipulate me.

It simply knows me perfectly.

Even so, why do I feel as though I am no longer the original?

I brought out the first answer again. I could choose not to give it, and yet I give it. The first half of that sentence had disappeared. Now I had no choice but to give it.

English key to the original diagram. Left, ‘Can turn it off’: a switch lies between the person and the SSOT; ‘I could withhold, yet I give.’ Right, ‘Cannot turn it off’: a locked, unbreakable connection; ‘I have no choice but to give.’ Neither side shows the SSOT directing the person’s behavior.

Figure 12. Neither diagram contains an arrow by which the SSOT directs my behavior. Only one thing has changed: the switch.

Choosing to give when I could withhold is different from having no choice but to give. The words I had said to the people at my company had come back to me. I have never called coming to work an act of agency when the person cannot resign.

Where the first answer falls apart

Here the path divides in two.

One path defends the first answer to the end. Agency lies in the freedom to cut off the flow, so people in a world without that freedom are no longer subjects of their own lives. The logic is tidy. The conclusion is strange. In that world, I still drink water, choose a route, disagree, and make a call. We would have to look at someone living just as they did yesterday and say that, because one switch has disappeared, the subject has disappeared, too.

The other path admits that the first answer was anchored in water too shallow.

I took the second path. If we stake agency only on the freedom to stop the logs, then human agency disappears the moment logging becomes compulsory. What I was looking for could not be something a single institutional rule or line in a set of terms could abolish.

This does not mean the switch is trivial. In the real world, I would stand on the side of protecting it. But the switch was a mechanism that protected agency; agency itself lived somewhere else. A lock protects a house, but nobody calls the lock the house.

So the question descends one step further.

Even without a right to refuse, do I, the biological being, still have agency?

There was another answer I could bring out: The Economics of Bearing the Consequences, which I had written earlier. There I had looked for what remains human in responsibility and bearing the consequences. My conclusion was that AI might judge and act, but could not take the consequences upon itself as part of its own life.

Even in a world without a switch, if something goes wrong, I am the person who stands in court. Could the fact that I am the being who bears the consequences answer this question?

Whether I can turn it off was my first answer to the question of agency. It could not be my last.

Figure 12 is reproduced from the Korean original, with an English reading key. The comparison table uses the existing English translation of the author’s source table. This essay is part of the Super Second Brain whitepaper.

items.title: Pharming Leadership Shake-Up Puts Shareholder Disclosure in Focus
items.author: Sanford Diday
items.content:
A leadership change needs a stated purpose. Shareholders deserve to know what the board intends it to accomplish, not merely who takes over.

On September 29, Pharming Group announced its chief executive’s departure, citing a disagreement over how to advance its strategy. According to the company, the board and CEO Fabrice Chouraqui agreed that their views on advancing the next phase of the strategy were “not sufficiently aligned” (Pharming Group, “Pharming Announces CEO Transition”).

“Not sufficiently aligned” states a reason for departure. It does not identify the disputed priority. That distinction matters: succession names the people taking charge; disclosure explains the purpose of the change.

Pharming announced continuity arrangements alongside the departure. Chief Commercial Officer Leverne Marsh and Chief Financial Officer Kenneth Lynard immediately became joint interim CEOs: Marsh leads patient-focused operations, and Lynard leads global corporate functions. The board began a formal search for a permanent successor. Chairman Richard Peters thanked Chouraqui for his service and identified continuity as the immediate priority (Pharming Group, “Pharming Announces CEO Transition”). The board moved quickly to ensure continuity, appointing two interim leaders and opening a permanent search.

Pharming said its strategy, pipeline, and commitment to patients remained unchanged (Pharming Group, “Pharming Announces CEO Transition”). Retaining a strategy still leaves choices about priorities, timing, and execution. In its September 29 article, De Belegger noted increased execution risk as Pharming worked to grow Joenja, stabilize RUCONEST, develop new indications, and control costs. That afternoon, the shares traded around €0.8886, down 3.4% from the previous day (“Pharming Zakt Weg”).

The financial context underscores the stakes. In its July 30 results, Pharming reduced its full-year revenue guidance by $30 million to a range of $375 million to $395 million. It also lowered its operating expense guidance by $15 million. Second quarter revenue fell 10% year over year for RUCONEST and grew 40% for Joenja (Pharming Group, “Pharming Reports Second Quarter and First Half 2026 Financial Results”). The October 27 update reported 21% third-quarter revenue growth overall, 14% for RUCONEST, and 58% for Joenja. It also reaffirmed narrowed annual revenue guidance of $380 million to $390 million (Pharming Group, “Pharming Group Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results”). Q3 growth aligns with Pharming’s stated commitment to its existing strategy. It supports the continuity claim, but it does not explain why the board changed leadership.

The October update also set operating goals: stabilize RUCONEST, expand Joenja, and obtain clinical data beyond APDS (Pharming Group, “Pharming Group Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results”). These goals establish what management intends to deliver. The September and October releases leave the connection between those goals and the leadership change unstated. Business objectives and the rationale for succession deserve separate scrutiny.

Shareholders do not need a transcript of the boardroom debate. Personnel matters and competitive plans demand discretion. The distinction is between explaining a decision’s purpose and exposing private deliberations. Meaningful disclosure addresses the first without demanding the second.

Operating results measure business performance. They do not replace the board’s explanation for why it changed leadership. Shareholders deserve a clear statement of the disputed priority, what the board intends the transition to accomplish, and how it will measure progress. Confidentiality protects deliberations. It does not replace accountability.

items.title: Publishing More Is Easy. Keeping AI Content Accurate Is Hard.
items.author: Pratik Thakker
items.content:
Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The difficult part of an AI content program may begin after publication. A product setting changes, a source is revised, or an approved claim expires. The team updates the main article while older versions continue circulating in slides, videos, newsletters, and downloadable guides.

Generation increased the number of assets. Maintenance did not increase at the same rate. The business now has a larger public surface carrying facts that nobody clearly owns.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would manage AI-assisted marketing content as a lifecycle with explicit release and correction states. The proposal is deliberately practical: know what is live, which evidence it depends on, who must review changes, and how the audience will receive a correction when one is necessary.

Define accuracy at the asset level

A source document can be correct while the published asset is not. A title may exaggerate the argument. An image may turn a hypothetical example into an apparent result. A metadata description may omit the condition that makes the headline defensible.

Treat the asset as the complete recipient-visible package. Review prose, headline, captions, tables, image labels, alt text, excerpts, previews, links, and attachments. Check the rendered version in the destination, not only the local document that was uploaded.

A useful acceptance question is whether a reader who encounters only that artifact will understand what the evidence actually supports. If the explanation depends on a hidden reviewer note or a qualification found only in a different asset, the public version needs revision.

Separate preparation from release

Drafted, reviewed, approved, scheduled, submitted, and live are different states. An editorial submission is not publication. A scheduling confirmation is not proof that the asset appeared correctly. A saved draft is not a promise that every field persisted.

Record the exact state with a timestamp and evidence from the owning system. A release checklist should require the team to reopen saved work and inspect the final preview. Where another publisher controls the final decision, keep that editorial state separate from the company's internal approval.

This may sound administrative, but it prevents a common reporting error: counting work that is prepared as work that reached an audience. It also gives the team a clear recovery point when an upload fails or a platform changes the asset during processing.

Build a dependency record alongside the draft

For each material factual claim, retain the source reference and the date it was checked. For each derivative, retain the source asset and revision. A small manifest can connect the article, diagram, newsletter, video script, and owned worksheet without requiring a complex publishing platform.

The W3C provenance overview provides a general model for origins and transformations. A content dependency record applies that idea to editorial maintenance; it does not automatically establish the truth of the underlying claim.

Use the record to answer a bounded question when something changes: which public artifacts contain this statement? Without that relationship, a correction becomes a search across folders, channels, and memory. The more assets a generation system produces, the more expensive that reconstruction can become.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Classify changes by consequence

A corrected spelling, an outdated feature requirement, and an unsupported customer outcome do not need the same response. Define categories that help the team prioritize work without minimizing material errors.

A cosmetic change may require a normal edit. A changed product condition may require the source and all affected derivatives to be reviewed. A materially misleading claim may require containment, a correction note, and separately approved communication to affected recipients.

Do not allow an automated classifier to make the final decision for consequential corrections without human review. The relevant question is what the audience could reasonably have understood and done because of the statement. A small wording change can have a large practical consequence when it concerns price, permissions, security, or customer commitments.

Make time part of the statement

Some content is intentionally historical. An article explaining what a product documented on a particular date should not be silently rewritten to imply it always described the current version. Other resources are intended as maintained implementation guides and need visible updates.

Choose the maintenance model before release. State when the documentation was checked, distinguish account-specific behavior, and avoid unsupported terms such as newly launched when no verified date is available. A future-looking argument should identify itself as analysis rather than fact about an inevitable outcome.

When updating an asset, retain a revision note proportionate to the change. Do not refresh the displayed date merely to imply freshness. The date should correspond to an actual review or material revision, with the supporting evidence retained in the editorial record.

Put review capacity into the production plan

If a team can generate twenty drafts but carefully inspect only four, the constraint is review capacity. Producing sixteen more unfinished assets does not remove it. It can make prioritization harder and increase pressure to approve work too quickly.

Plan for verification, design inspection, source checks, platform preview, and maintenance. Assign named owners before expanding the batch. Measure rework and rejection reasons so the team can improve inputs rather than repeatedly correcting the same class of mistake.

Google's generative-content guidance warns against producing many pages without user value. The relevant planning lesson is not a particular volume limit. It is that production count cannot substitute for a useful contribution and a review process capable of supporting it.

Test the workflow with deliberately flawed inputs

Use synthetic drafts containing known problems: an unsupported number, an expired credential, a broken link, a caption that changes the meaning of a chart, a missing disclosure, and a source that does not support the adjacent sentence.

Test the entire workflow. Can the issue survive research, writing, design, metadata entry, and upload? Does the final reviewer see it in the rendered preview? Does the system hold the asset rather than merely add a warning that someone ignores?

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework supports a risk-management approach to AI systems. This proposed editorial fixture set is limited to the cases tested. Passing it does not establish that future content is error-free or that a tool is certified for public publishing.

Keep access controls separate from editorial approval

An assistant may be allowed to read a source without being allowed to publish it. A user may have permission to save a draft without authority to send a message or release a story. The workflow should preserve both distinctions.

HubSpot's AI-settings documentation describes feature and data-source controls. Those controls do not decide whether an individual claim or final external communication has been approved.

Maintain a separate release gate with the appropriate scope. For sensitive customer material, review the evidence and publication permission. For an external email, review the actual sender, recipients, subject, body, links, and attachments. Do not interpret approval of a project as approval of every future recipient-visible action.

Design for partial correction

Some surfaces allow editing. Others preserve sent copies, cached previews, screenshots, or syndicated versions. A correction plan must acknowledge that not every copy can be replaced.

Map the available actions by surface: edit, append a correction, replace an asset, update a destination, contact a publisher, or communicate with affected recipients under the organization's approval process. Preserve a record of the original issue and the verified repair.

Do not call an attempted edit a completed correction until the destination has been reopened. Check that the revised text, image, and preview actually display. Where a platform controls publication, record the request and the unresolved state instead of claiming that a change is live because it was submitted.

Measure maintenance quality

Useful operational measures include unresolved material claims, overdue source reviews, time to contain a confirmed issue, affected derivatives still awaiting repair, and repeated failure categories. Define each measure so another reviewer can reproduce it.

Avoid optimizing for an artificially low error count by discouraging discovery. A team that finds and fixes a problem may be improving the system. A team that never examines older assets may simply have less visibility into its errors.

Review the causes, not only the totals. Repeated factual errors may indicate weak source selection. Repeated visual mistakes may indicate an inadequate design check. Repeated metadata problems may indicate a platform workflow issue. Each deserves a different intervention and a test that confirms the repair.

Review the release under realistic reading conditions

A local document can hide problems that appear on the destination. A table may overflow on a narrow screen. A code block may lose formatting. A social crop may remove the label that identifies an example as hypothetical. A metadata preview may substitute an outdated image.

Inspect the artifact where the audience will encounter it, at a useful reading size. Check the opening, the practical framework, the important qualification, and the final next step. Verify that a linked file opens and contains the expected version. Where a platform transcodes images or changes markup, record the resulting limitation rather than claiming exact parity with the source.

Keep the inspection proportionate to the asset's consequence, but do not replace it with an automated green indicator. A checklist may confirm that an image exists without confirming that it is the right image. A source-count test may confirm four links without confirming that they support the claims.

Use automation for deterministic checks and human inspection for meaning and rendering. The two layers complement each other. Neither should be represented as a complete substitute for the other, particularly when an external platform transforms the submitted material.

Give every asset an owner after publication

Publishing should not be the moment responsibility ends. Assign an owner for monitoring consequential dependencies, reviewing reader corrections, and deciding whether the resource should be updated or retired. The owner does not need to inspect every asset every day; review frequency should reflect volatility and risk.

When a resource is retired, decide what happens to incoming links and related materials. A replacement should satisfy the same reader need where possible. Do not redirect every obsolete educational page to a generic sales destination and call that maintenance.

AI makes it easier to create a large content surface. A lifecycle makes that surface supportable. The strategic advantage is not maximum output. It is the ability to keep useful work accurate, traceable, and correctable after the initial excitement of publication has passed.

For a related evidence boundary, see Designing a Claim-Validation Workflow for AI-Generated Customer Emails. The framework above addresses a distinct marketing decision rather than repeating that model.

Sources checked October 21, 2026. Proposed process states and test cases are illustrative. No external content was published for this article.

items.title: How Congo's Mineral Wealth Could Shape Its Role in AI
items.author: tt
items.content:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo enters the geopolitics of artificial intelligence through the physical systems on which computation depends. Its mineral production gives the country a substantial place in several industrial supply chains. The strategic question is whether that position can support a wider domestic capability: reliable electricity, technical employment, processing expertise and institutions able to negotiate and enforce durable agreements.

That question directs attention to decisions made after extraction. A country can supply an important material while purchasing the equipment, finance and technical services needed to use it. It can also host a large mine without exercising equivalent control over the firms, contracts and downstream facilities connecting that mine to customers.

What the production figures establish

The US Geological Survey estimates Congolese cobalt mine production at 230,000 tonnes of contained metal in 2025. Its tantalum table puts the country at 1,300 tonnes, against a rounded world total of 2,500 tonnes: approximately 52%. These figures establish production weight within two different mineral markets.[1][2]

Neither measure is a share of the AI economy. Cobalt serves several industrial uses, including batteries; tantalum is used in high-reliability electronic components. Copper connects the country to the wider electrical economy. The relationship with AI runs through specific components, power systems and equipment, alongside demand from many other industries.[1][2][3]

The relevant dependence therefore has to be established for each material and production stage. A buyer's exposure to a Congolese mine may differ substantially from its exposure to the refiner or component producer further along the chain. Production geography alone cannot identify which actor can alter access to the finished product.

Where bargaining power meets dependence

Export policy demonstrates one means by which the government can influence a market. USGS records a temporary cobalt export ban in February 2025, followed by quotas in October. The same source identifies China as the leading producer of refined cobalt.[1] Extraction and refining therefore need separate treatment, as do the location of a mine and the ownership of its operator.

My assessment is that Congolese bargaining power is strongest when policy decisions are connected to credible domestic alternatives. Restrictions can alter access to material, but they also create costs that companies and buyers may respond to through stocks, investment or substitution. The national benefit depends on contract terms, revenue collection, enforcement and the country's ability to sustain a negotiated position.

A useful country profile should consequently ask who is negotiating, which obligations are enforceable and what remains locally when the transaction is complete. Export revenues, training commitments and an operating processing facility represent different forms of benefit. They should be reported separately.

An industrial route with achievable steps

The World Bank's 2023 study of mining and battery value chains examines opportunities for additional processing and copper-based products, while identifying electricity, transport, finance and institutional capacity as constraints.[3] It provides a diagnosis of possible industrial pathways, rather than evidence that the proposed facilities have since been delivered.

An achievable route would select investments against those constraints. A project making electrical products for identifiable regional customers could build engineering and supplier capabilities. More complex processing could follow where power, logistics and commercial demand justify it. Each step needs a customer, an operating budget and a workforce capable of maintaining the equipment.

Electricity is central to that assessment. The national Mission 300 progress report, published for the first quarter of 2026, records 652,000 additional people gaining access during 2025.[4] This is a reported access outcome. Industrial reliability requires additional evidence about outages, available capacity and service at the locations where a project would operate.

The distinction matters for public investment. An announcement can establish a commitment, construction can establish progress and a commissioned plant can establish availability. Sustained production and local learning require a further record. Country coverage should follow that sequence instead of treating the initial announcement as the final result.

The framework's Industrialisation layer captures the country's material contribution. Operationalisation asks what Congolese organisations could do with AI themselves. Candidate uses include equipment maintenance, electricity demand planning and administrative document processing. These are proposed applications, not verified national deployments.

A credible pilot would start with a defined task and an accountable organisation. It would require usable data, trained staff, secure access and a way to compare performance with the existing process. Contracts should make clear who maintains the system, who can inspect its outputs and whether the organisation can change suppliers without losing its working records.

Invention remains relevant through local engineering, research and adaptation. A mining or energy organisation that develops evaluation skills may become a more capable purchaser and user of technology. That is a specific institutional gain, even where the underlying model and hardware come from abroad.

What would demonstrate progress

The next indicators should concern conversion: facilities that sustain production, local suppliers securing repeat contracts, technical staff maintaining systems and public organisations documenting useful deployments. Transparent reporting on electricity reliability and the implementation of mineral agreements would strengthen that assessment.

The DRC could occupy a more consequential position in the AI economy by connecting mineral production to these domestic capabilities. The opportunity is conditional, and its success will be visible in organisations that can perform tasks more reliably, retain knowledge and negotiate from a stronger position.

This is original country analysis applying the GOAI capability conversion framework. It is not a peer-reviewed country assessment or a scored ranking. Proposed applications and indicators are analytical judgments; company and government claims are attributed to their sources.

items.title: Why Building Multiple AI Agents Requires More Than Copying the Same Brain
items.author: Hanul Lee (이하늘)
items.content:
I had a brain. The next question was who would use it, and how.

The easiest route is duplication: produce as many agents as needed with the same brain, the same instructions, and the same way of speaking.

That is what I did at first.

Ten identical agents notice the same things and miss the same things.

It is like sending ten people into a meeting and receiving ten identical sets of notes.

Think of a company, and the answer becomes clearer.

Members of a good organization share the same history and vision, but the finance lead and the sales lead hear different things in the same meeting.

That difference broadens the organization’s field of view.

One meeting, three sets of notes

So I designed the agents to share the entire SSOT while each retained a perspective of its own.

Their assigned roles, what they notice first, accumulated experiences, and habitual ways of judging things all differ.

After the same meeting, the scene looks like this.

“There are three follow-up actions. One needs a reply by Thursday.”

“The market-size figure they gave needs verification. I have formulated two hypotheses.”

“This proposal conflicts with our direction for this year. Even if we accept it, the terms need to change.”

All three sets of notes came from the same SSOT. All three agents know my values and the company’s context. They are simply standing in different places.

This is what interested me about frameworks such as Letta.

In brief, Letta is an open-source agent framework that grew out of the MemGPT paper by researchers at UC Berkeley.

Its starting point was an analogy with an operating system.

Just as a computer moves between limited memory and a larger disk, an agent moves between memories currently open in front of it and memories filed away.

What matters is that the agent does the organizing itself.

It keeps notes close at hand about “what kind of agent I am” and “who the person I help is.” If it decides while working that a note is wrong, it revises the note itself.

The agent does not disappear when the conversation ends.

It returns the next day with notes a little different from yesterday’s.

If Hindsight in Chapter 1 showed how memory can rework itself, Letta showed that the agent itself could be the owner of that memory.

This starts from somewhere different from making an agent imitate a role through a few lines of system prompt.

An agent accumulates memories of its own over time and develops an identity.

The research agent remembers a hypothesis it made three months ago that proved wrong, and is a little more cautious this time.

These are the scenes I meant in the prologue when I wrote that even the bots were developing a stubborn streak of their own.

The three sets of notes above illustrate role-specific interpretation. Letta documents editable memory and configurations in which agents share memory while retaining their own context. The language of identity and a stubborn streak in this essay is the author’s interpretation of that architecture.

English key to the original diagram. REAL (events in the world) → SSOT → perspectives (each agent’s lens) → a group of agents → actions (emails, meetings, decisions) → REAL. At the center: action becomes reality, and reality becomes the brain again. The green arrow runs from REAL back to the SSOT.

Figure 6. The traces an agent leaves in the world become the agent’s brain again. The green arrow marks where the loop closes.

The point to watch in this diagram is where the arrow comes back.

When an agent sends an email, that email becomes an event in the world. The recipient replies, a meeting is scheduled, a contract moves forward. All of it flows back into REAL and revises the SSOT.

At first, almost all the input circulating through this loop came from me: the people I met, the things I said, the decisions I made.

As the number of agents grows, my share of the data moving through the loop becomes smaller.

That changing proportion is the subject of the next chapter.

A super second brain differs from an army of copies of one brain. It is an organization that interprets the same brain in different ways.

Which different perspectives would you give agents that share the same memory?

This essay is the English translation of Chapter 3 of , an ongoing Korean whitepaper series by Hanul Lee, with an added source note. Read the Korean series on Substack. items.title: Polymarket Halted International Trading After Hackers Drained Accounts
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Trading has resumed on Polymarket's flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders. A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market's website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.
 
On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; Blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appear affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but said it will refund impacted traders.
 
The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company's newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries. This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced losses like this. "A nearly identical vendor-compromise attack hit the platform in June, draining close to $3 million from at least 11 user wallets through the same kind of injected frontend script," reports StartupFortune.
 
Hours before Polymarket halted trading, more than $2 billion in cryptocurrency was drained from Binance wallets in just 40 minutes.

items.title: How ASML Gives the Netherlands a Strategic Advantage in Global AI
items.author: tt
items.content:
The Netherlands can influence the development of AI far beyond the size of its domestic market. The source of that influence is a specialised industrial position: the machinery and knowledge needed to manufacture advanced semiconductors. ASML places the country close to an important constraint on the expansion of computing capacity. Yet the Dutch government cannot treat the company's technology, suppliers and customers as resources available for unrestricted national use. The strategic question concerns the terms on which this commercial position can support public objectives, and the costs of doing so.

A position inside production

ASML reported €32.7 billion in net sales and €4.7 billion in research and development expenditure for 2025. Its reported system sales included 48 extreme ultraviolet lithography systems. These figures establish the scale of an industrial organisation; they do not measure Dutch state capability. A machine sold to a customer becomes part of a production process whose location, ownership and operational priorities may lie elsewhere. [1]

The distinction becomes clearer through three layers: Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation. Invention concerns the knowledge and technical advances that expand what AI systems and their underlying technologies can do. Industrialisation concerns the production and infrastructure that make those advances reproducible at scale. Operationalisation concerns their sustained use by organisations pursuing concrete objectives. Governance connects these layers through funding, access rules, procurement and institutional responsibility.

The Netherlands has a particularly consequential position where invention becomes industrial production. The joint ASML–imec High NA EUV laboratory, opened in Veldhoven in June 2024, gave chipmakers and equipment and materials suppliers access to a prototype scanner and associated tools. The stated purpose was preparation for manufacturing. [2] Such arrangements matter because a promising technical design becomes strategically useful only when multiple organisations can make it work reliably together.

The international foundations of Dutch influence

ASML's 2025 reporting describes a supplier network of 5,100 organisations: 1,600 in the Netherlands, 700 elsewhere in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, 1,350 in North America, and 1,450 in Asia. These are supplier counts, without weights for expenditure or technical importance. [1] They establish geographical breadth, while leaving the concentration of critical dependencies to more detailed analysis.

The company also reports that approximately 80% of its bill of materials comes from external suppliers and describes its optical collaboration with ZEISS. [3] This makes the policy problem reciprocal. Countries and firms seeking advanced manufacturing equipment depend on capabilities assembled around ASML; ASML also depends on capabilities beyond Dutch territory. Sustaining influence therefore requires cooperation with the partners whose contributions keep that position technically credible.

What the state can decide

Export authorisation provides a concrete mechanism linking commercial capability to public authority. In January 2025, the Dutch government announced an extension of its national controls to specified measuring and inspection equipment, effective from April. The announcement explained that applications would be assessed individually for destinations outside the EU and distinguished authorisation requirements from a general prohibition. [4]

This mechanism gives the state an intervention point. It does not establish control over every stage of semiconductor production or guarantee that a restriction will achieve its intended strategic result. That result depends on which technologies are covered, the availability of substitutes, enforcement and the decisions of other supplier countries. Judging Dutch influence requires examining these conditions rather than inferring political power directly from company revenue.

The same state also has to maintain the conditions for production at home. Project Beethoven, announced in March 2024, committed a €2.51 billion package to the semiconductor ecosystem, including education, accessibility, housing and spatial infrastructure. The government explicitly connected the package to keeping the Netherlands attractive for ASML's investment. [5] This was an announced policy commitment; its financial scale alone does not demonstrate completed delivery or resolved bottlenecks.

From industrial importance to usable capability

For Dutch ministries and public organisations, the operational question remains separate: which AI capabilities can they access, maintain and use for their own tasks? Hosting an influential equipment producer does not automatically provide a ministry with dependable computing capacity, suitable models or the staff needed to integrate them into public services. Those connections require decisions and budgets of their own.

There is an industrial route to deeper capability. ASML describes the use of AI in engineering, computational lithography and maintenance in its 2025 reporting. [3] This illustrates how knowledge generated within a production ecosystem can also improve its operations. The national opportunity is conditional: research partnerships, training and procurement must help relevant expertise circulate while respecting commercial knowledge and security requirements. The benefits cannot be assumed to spread throughout the economy unaided.

What would change the assessment

Four observable developments would clarify the Netherlands' trajectory. First, changes in licensing decisions and equipment deliveries would reveal how export policy affects actual access. Second, disclosures on critical supplier capacity and substitution would show whether international dependence is becoming more manageable. Third, completed education, housing and infrastructure measures would indicate whether Project Beethoven is relieving the constraints it identified. Fourth, documented public and industrial AI deployments would show whether technical strength is translating into sustained organisational performance.

The Netherlands can remain an influential partner in the governance and supply of advanced production technologies. That role depends on preserving the engineering ecosystem while making selective, credible decisions about access. Its strongest strategic asset is the ability to participate in decisions others cannot easily disregard. Converting that position into broader national capability requires work beyond the semiconductor equipment industry itself.
